article_title: Assessing ELA and Math Curriculum Shifts: A Practical Guide for Measurement and Progress Monitoring
citation: Assessing ELA and Math Curriculum Shifts: A Practical Guide for Measurement and Progress Monitoring. Shared Measures Construct Map.
title: Bidirectional and unidirectional relations among curriculum-shift dimensions
description: The construct map's KEY distinguishes "Unidirectional" and "Bidirectional" relations among its six dimensions, presenting the system as an interconnected progression rather than a linear checklist. Dimensions such as instructional leadership, teacher professional learning, teacher mindsets and beliefs, teacher instructional practice, and student outcomes are linked so that change in one dimension relates to others, with some relations running in both directions. This pattern guides how users read and score the map during progress monitoring.
requirements: Users must consult the map's KEY to identify which dimension-to-dimension relations are unidirectional and which are bidirectional
constraints: The printed document does not enumerate which specific pairs of dimensions carry each relation type
target_learning_goals: system-level monitoring of curriculum implementation
examples: The KEY prints the labels "Unidirectional" and "Bidirectional" alongside the note "Items specific to ELA and Math"

article_title: Bilingual Beginnings: Planning Kindergarten Entry Assessments for Spanish-English Speakers
citation: Rolla, A., & Mottesi, G. (2024). Bilingual Beginnings: Planning Kindergarten Entry Assessments for Spanish–English Speakers. WestEd, Region 15 Comprehensive Center. https://csaa.wested.org/resource/kindergarten-entry-assessments-an-examination-of-best-practices-national-trends-and-recommendations/
title: Use bilingual profiles—assessments covering proficiency in both English and the home language—to identify supports and close opportunity gaps for Spanish–English bilingual kindergarteners
description: A bilingual profile is a detailed assessment including a student's proficiency in English and home language(s), literacy skills, and other developmental areas, providing a comprehensive picture of strengths and needs. The brief argues states should implement policies facilitating bilingual profiles because "These bilingual profiles can more accurately identify what supports students need, allowing states and districts to close opportunity gaps more effectively." Profiles should draw on skills and lived experiences in both languages, with continued screening allowing flexible categorization that avoids stigmatizing labels.
requirements: Assessment information must be usable at state, district, community, school, and classroom levels to inform equitable resource allocation and targeted, culturally and linguistically responsive interventions.
constraints: Including Spanish and English versions in all assessed domains may increase administration time and limit teacher capacity to collect evidence for specific areas; differences in home-language use policies across states and districts can affect reliability and validity.
target_learners: Spanish–English bilingual kindergarteners, including those classified as English Learners
target_learning_goals: School readiness in language, literacy, and mathematics; accurate identification of needed supports and interventions in both languages
examples: The brief recommends that states implement policies facilitating bilingual profiles and tailor assessments and instructional strategies to the unique needs of Spanish–English bilinguals across both languages.

article_title: Expanding Equitable Access to Bilingual Education in California's Silicon Valley: Analysis and Recommendations
citation: Expanding Equitable Access to Bilingual Education in California's Silicon Valley: Analysis and Recommendations. (2026). https://www.wested.org
title: Conditions-for-success framework: additive bilingualism and shared bilingual conditions benefit all English Learner programs, not only formal bilingual models
description: The report organizes its analysis around a set of conditions critical to the success of any program for English Learners, treating bilingual educational opportunity as "a range of conditions that are critical to the success of all educational programs for students who are English Learners." Central to this is additive bilingualism, "an approach whereby students acquire English while maintaining and developing their home language." The framework holds that conditions such as bilingually authorized staff assignment, staff who value other languages and cultures, home language learning opportunities, and partnerships with multilingual families support success in any English Learner program and create foundations for formal bilingual programs.
requirements: Assignment of bilingual instructors, which the report calls a requirement for bilingual programs that increases support for English Learner students in any type of program
constraints: The report notes LCAPs provide only limited information on English Learner program investments regionwide
target_learners: English Learner and Multilingual Learner students in K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: Bilingualism and biliteracy development alongside academic content learning in English and a partner language
examples: The study used this framework to examine how bilingual educational opportunities are reflected in Silicon Valley English Learner programs and resource allocation

article_title: Growing Strong Learners in Galt Joint Union Elementary School District
citation: McCarthy, E., Morgan, C. & Sussman, J. (2020). Growing strong learners in Galt Joint Union Elementary School District. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org

The article states the BCOAs "answered questions for parents; reminded them of upcoming events, activities, and deadlines; forwarded helpful resources to parents; assisted parents in the enrollment process; and provided language interpreting for parents." BCOAs also hosted outreach events, supported EL parent leadership, coordinated recruitment, and, during COVID-19 closure, made weekly check-in calls, ran a daily tech hotline, and delivered distance-learning packets, Chromebooks, and hotspots to homes.

constraints: During school closure the role shifted to remote supports such as phone calls and home delivery of resources
target_learners: Pre-K English learner and migrant children and their Spanish-language-dominant families
target_learning_goals: Family engagement, kindergarten transition preparation, and parent leadership development
examples: Administrators reported BCOAs interpreted during IEP meetings and parent conferences, facilitated APTT meetings, and built rapport with parents who otherwise might have a hard time connecting with school personnel

article_title: Striving for Relationship-Centered Schools: Insights from a Community-Based Transformation Campaign
citation: Hernández, L. H., & Rivero, E. (2023). Striving for relationship-centered schools: Insights from a community-based transformation campaign. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/621.856
title: Biweekly homerooms as relationship-centered small communities
description: McLane High School transformed its homeroom structure as a core RCS effort to build consistent relationships in a large school. The report explains that "Biweekly homeroom periods aimed to form small communities for McLane's large student population and enable consistent, multiyear connections." Professional development for educators on homeroom practices

article_title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later
citation: Sweller, J., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 261–292. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09465-5
title: Biologically primary versus biologically secondary knowledge distinction grounds cognitive load theory in evolutionary educational psychology
description: Post-1998 CLT categorises knowledge using Geary's distinction: biologically primary knowledge is evolved, acquired effortlessly and automatically without explicit teaching, and is modular; biologically secondary knowledge is culturally determined, domain-specific, and requires conscious effort and explicit instruction. The article states that "All secondary knowledge tends to require conscious effort on the part of the learner and explicit instruction on the part of an instructor." Educational institutions exist because of the need to acquire secondary knowledge.
requirements: Biologically secondary skills must be explicitly taught and actively learned
constraints: Attempts to teach purely generic-cognitive (primary) skills lead to dead-ends, per Sala and Gobet as cited; primary skills can only assist, not substitute for, secondary learning
target_learners: students in education and training contexts
target_learning_goals: acquisition of domain-specific biologically secondary knowledge
examples: The SBAR communication method for medical emergency teams: speaking is primary, but the specific SBAR reporting procedure is secondary and teachable

citation: Roessingh, H. (2006). BICS-CALP: An Introduction for Some, a Review for Others. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, 23(2), Spring 2006. https://www.tesl.ca
title: Cummins' BICS-CALP framework as a four-quadrant developmental continuum overlaid on an iceberg metaphor
description: The article presents an adapted version of Cummins' (1982) framework in which context (embedded to reduced) forms the horizontal axis and cognitive demand (undemanding to demanding) the vertical axis, yielding four quadrants from BICS to CALP. The author overlays this on an iceberg image: "Like an iceberg, BICS may represent only about 10% of the overall proficiency of an academically competent learner." Quadrants 1-2 are BICS, quadrant 3 is transitional, and quadrant 4 involves metaphoric competence.
requirements: Understanding the role of first-language proficiency and age on arrival is described as key to understanding the relationship between above- and below-the-surface features
constraints: The author presents it as her own adaptation of Cummins' original framework and notes it is a work in progress

target_learning_goals: Development of cognitive academic language proficiency (CALP) in English as a second language
examples: The article maps quadrant contents: quadrant 1 covers survival chunks and 1,000-2,500 high-frequency words; quadrant 4 requires 12,000+ words and extensive academic reading and writing

article_title: Sex Differences in Performance on the Mathematics Section of the Scholastic Aptitude Test: A Bidirectional Validity Study
citation: Howard Wainer, Linda Steinberg. (1992). Sex Differences in Performance on the Mathematics Section of the Scholastic Aptitude Test: A Bidirectional Validity Study. Harvard Educational Review. https://doi.org/10.17763/haer.62.3.1p1555011301r133
title: Bidirectional validity study: evaluating a test by matching examinees on the criterion the test predicts
description: The bidirectional validity approach examines a test's fairness by working backward from the criterion: examinees are matched on the outcome the test is supposed to predict (here, type of math course taken and grade received in first-year college math), and their test scores are compared. Wainer and Steinberg apply it to the SAT-M with "almost 47,000 men and women" and complement it with a prospective regression analysis of the same data. Differences in test scores among equally performing examinees indicate differences in the test's predictive validity across groups.
requirements: Requires a large dataset linking test scores to the criterion performance (course taken and grade received) so examinees can be matched on outcome.
constraints: The article states the data do not allow conclusions about the cause of the observed score differences.
target_learners: college students taking first-year mathematics courses
target_learning_goals: accurate and equitable prediction of college mathematics performance from admissions test scores
examples: Matching almost 47,000 men and women on type of math course taken and grade received, then comparing SAT-M scores; a prospective regression analysis of the same data.

article_title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
citation: Chan, C. K. Y., & Hu, W. (2023). Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:43. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00411-8
title: Biggs' 3P (Presage–Process–Product) model as the framework linking student perceptions of GenAI to learning approaches and outcomes
description: The article adopts John Biggs' 3P (Presage–Process–Product) model as its explanatory framework: "students’ perceptions of their learning environment, their abilities, and the teaching strategies used have a significant impact on their approach to learning", which in turn influences outcomes. Positive perceptions foster a deep approach seeking understanding and connections; negative perceptions foster a surface approach focused on memorizing minimum requirements. The authors use this to argue that understanding students' GenAI perceptions lets educators tailor integration so students adopt a deep approach.
requirements: Requires attention to how students perceive the learning environment, including technologies such as GenAI, when designing teaching and assessment
constraints: The model is applied interpretively; the study did not test the model's predictions about GenAI use empirically
target_learning_goals: deep approaches to learning, effective integration of GenAI into teaching and learning
examples: The authors argue that when students perceive GenAI as a valuable and supportive resource they are more likely to adopt a deep approach to learning, and that perception insights can inform institutional GenAI guidelines.

description: This principle holds that universally designed digital learning environments should make every text and activity available in students' two languages rather than translating only selected materials. article_title: Two is better than one: bilingual education promotes the flexible mind
citation: I.K. Christoffels, L. Steenbergen, W.P.M. van den Wildenberg, L.S. Colzato. (2015). Two is better than one: bilingual education promotes the flexible mind. Psychological Research, 79(3), 371-379. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00426-014-0575-3
title: Bilingual language use requires and trains a flexible mindset for rapid switching between languages
description: The article's explanatory account holds that managing two languages places demands on cognitive control: "Speaking two languages (or more) requires people to develop a flexible mindset to rapidly switch back and forth between languages". On this view, the daily practice of moving between languages exercises domain-general cognitive flexibility, which is why the authors predicted and found smaller switching costs and a reduced global precedence effect in bilingually educated students. The study is offered as support for the idea that bilingual education promotes cognitive flexibility.
requirements: Sustained use of and switching between two languages, as in bilingual education programs, to exercise the flexible mindset
target_learners: High-school students in bilingual education programs
target_learning_goals: Development of cognitive flexibility and attentional control through bilingual language use
examples: The authors predicted that bilingually educated students would show smaller switching costs and a decreased global precedence effect, and reported both results
key_sources: I.K. Christoffels, L. Steenbergen, W.P.M. van den Wildenberg, L.S. Colzato. (2015). Two is better than one: bilingual education promotes the flexible mind. Psychological Research, 79(3), 371-379. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00426-014-0575-3

article_title: Two is better than one: bilingual education promotes the flexible mind
citation: I.K. Christoffels, L. Steenbergen, W.P.M. van den Wildenberg, L.S. Colzato. (2015). Two is better than one: bilingual education promotes the flexible mind. Psychological Research, 79(3), 371-379. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00426-014-0575-3
title: Offer bilingual education to promote students' cognitive flexibility and a focused scope of attention
description: The article recommends bilingual education as a route to cognitive benefits: "Our findings support the idea that bilingual education promotes cognitive flexibility and a bias towards a more focused 'scope' of attention". Teaching students in both English and Dutch, rather than only in Dutch, was associated with smaller switching costs and a decreased global precedence effect on a well-established switching paradigm. The principle treats the bilingual curriculum itself as the design lever for these executive advantages.
requirements: Instruction delivered in two languages (English and Dutch in this study) rather than a single-language regular curriculum
constraints: Evidence comes from a comparison of two groups of Dutch high-school students on one paradigm; the abstract reports no effect sizes
target_learning_goals: Cognitive flexibility
Focused attentional scope
examples: Dutch high-school students followed either regular classes in Dutch or were taught in both English and Dutch, and completed a global–local switching paradigm

article_title: The Impact of Bilingualism on Executive Functions in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review Based on the PRISMA Method
citation: Giovannoli J, Martella D, Federico F, Pirchio S and Casagrande M (2020) The Impact of Bilingualism on Executive Functions in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review Based on the PRISMA Method. Front. Psychol. 11:574789. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.574789
title: Bilingual advantage theory: constant control of two co-active languages trains executive functions
description: The bilingual advantage theory holds that because both of a bilingual's languages remain active, constantly controlling them to select the context-appropriate one acts as continuous training for executive functions. The review presents this as the theory whose empirical support it evaluates, tracing it to Green's Joint Activation Model, in which a general suppression mechanism inhibits the non-target language. The review frames it as the most controversial topic in bilingualism research.
requirements: Studies must compare bilingual and monolingual groups on executive function measures to test the theory's predictions
constraints: The review reports that results are controversial and that the term bilingual advantage has been questioned in favor of the more neutral term bilingual effect
target_learning_goals: executive function development: inhibition, cognitive flexibility, working memory
key_sources: Giovannoli J, Martella D, Federico F, Pirchio S and Casagrande M (2020) The Impact of Bilingualism on Executive Functions in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review Based on the PRISMA Method. Front. Psychol. 11:574789. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.574789

article_title: Perspective-taking ability in bilingual children: Extending advantages in executive control to spatial reasoning
citation: Greenberg Anastasia, Bellana Buddhika, Bialystok Ellen. (2013). Perspective-Taking Ability in Bilingual Children: Extending Advantages in Executive Control to Spatial Reasoning. Cognitive Development. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogdev.2012.10.002
title: Bilingual executive-control advantage arises from managing jointly activated languages via domain-general inhibitory control
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that for bilinguals "both languages are jointly activated for bilinguals, even in strongly monolingual contexts", creating a need for attentional control of the target language. In Green's (1998) model, this selective attention recruits a domain-general inhibitory control system, and the authors argue this trained control generalizes to nonverbal tasks such as perspective taking. The article also cites Costa and colleagues' monitoring account as a broader alternative.
requirements: Bilingual experience with two actively managed languages, producing joint activation that requires a control mechanism
constraints: Some inhibition types show no bilingual advantage, and advantages appear in infants where active inhibition of a competing language is not relevant, so the article treats inhibition alone as insufficient
target_learning_goals: executive control
spatial perspective taking
academic problem solving
examples: The study tested the account's prediction that bilinguals would outperform monolinguals on a perspective-taking task relying on executive control but not verbal proficiency.
key_sources: Greenberg Anastasia, Bellana Buddhika, Bialystok Ellen. (2013). Perspective-Taking Ability in Bilingual Children: Extending Advantages in Executive Control to Spatial Reasoning. Cognitive Development. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogdev.2012.10.002

article_title: Associations between preschool language and first grade reading outcomes in bilingual children
citation: Davison, Megan Dunn; Hammer, Carol; Lawrence, Frank R. (2011). Associations between Preschool Language and First Grade Reading Outcomes in Bilingual Children. Journal of Communication Disorders. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3138808/
title: Longitudinal bilingual language and literacy dataset from 81 Head Start children with growth curve analysis
description: The study's dataset comprises 81 bilingual Puerto Rican-heritage children from low-income families in Central Pennsylvania, assessed in fall and spring of two Head Start years and at the end of first grade. Language measures included the TELD-3 and PPVT-III for English, the PLS-3 and TVIP for Spanish, and the WLPB-R letter-word identification and passage comprehension subtests for reading. Children were divided into Home English Communicators (n = 48) and School English Communicators (n = 33) based on mothers' reports of English exposure timing. Growth curve models were estimated using R-software 2.5.1 with measurement occasion as the time metric.
requirements: Participants were typically-developing children who passed hearing and developmental screenings and were eligible for two years of Head Start
constraints: Approximately 20% of children could not be located over the four-year period; language tests were standardized on monolingual populations
target_learners: bilingual preschool children from low-income families
target_learning_goals: predicting first-grade reading outcomes from preschool language growth
examples: Raw scores were used instead of standard scores because standard scores based on monolingual norms would reflect little change for typically-developing children

article_title: Trajectories of parental engagement in early childhood among dual-earner families: Effects on child self-control.
citation: Tiago Ferreira, Joana Cadima, Marisa Matias, Joana Marina Vieira, and Teresa Leal; Karine Verschueren; Paula Mena Matos. (2018). Trajectories of Parental Engagement in Early Childhood Among Dual-Earner Families: Effects on Child Self-Control. Developmental Psychology, 54(4), 731–743. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000458
title: Ecological and bioecological framing of parental engagement as a proximal process supporting self-regulation
description: The article frames parental engagement within Bronfenbrenner's bioecological theory, where "human development is driven by reciprocal interactive processes between the developing person and its complex environment." Parent-child shared activities in positive engagement (play, outings, joint projects) are described as "unique opportunities for parents to provide their children with adaptive models of behavioral regulation." Parents act as external regulators of children's emotions and behaviors, supporting internalization of self-control. This framework positions the work-family mesosystem as a context that can either support or undermine these proximal processes through parents' perceived work-family conflict.
requirements: Parents must have opportunities for direct, positive, dyadic interaction with the child in activities that pose emotional challenges
constraints: The framework is applied specifically to dual-earner families with children in the preschool-to-first-grade period in this study
target_learners: four-year-old children in dual-earner families transitioning from preschool to first grade
target_learning_goals: behavioral self-control
emotion regulation in social interactions
socioemotional competence
examples: The study measured engagement via parent reports on the PRQ involvement subscale covering planning free time together, outings, outdoor activities, games, and joint projects

article_title: The Social Origins of Human Prosociality
citation: Dahl A., Brownell C. A. (2019). The Social Origins of Human Prosociality. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0963721419830386
title: Bidirectional socialization account: prosocial motives develop through two-way caregiver-infant interactions rather than being inherent
description: This framework holds that human infants are "ultrasocial" and open to learning through social exchange from birth, and that helping emerges amid affectively positive participation in games, chores, and cooperative activities. Interactions are bidirectional: infants actively elicit support and guidance, and caregivers adapt their scaffolding to infants' developing competence. The authors conclude that "infants are not inherently prosocial, but gradually develop prosocial motives through various types of bidirectional interactions in the first two years of life," positioning this against accounts that grant parents limited roles.
requirements: Caregivers who respond to infants' initiatives and support their participation in everyday activities, since without such participation and guidance infant helping would not emerge
constraints: The account focuses on interactions with adult caregivers, which the authors call central early on, though peer and sibling interactions also matter
target_learners: infants and toddlers in the first two years of life
target_learning_goals: emergence of helping, sharing, and comforting behavior and of prosocial motives
examples: Naturalistic research showing helping commonly begins when infants watch adults, whereupon adults encourage and assist them in joining the activity; parents do not insist on participation but support it when infants show interest.
key_sources: Dahl A., Brownell C. A. (2019). The Social Origins of Human Prosociality. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0963721419830386

article_title: Spatial activity participation in childhood and adolescence: consistency and relations to spatial thinking in adolescence
citation: Emily Grossnickle Peterson, Adam B. Weinberger, David H. Uttal, Bob Kolvoord and Adam E. Green. (2020). Spatial activity participation in childhood and adolescence: consistency and relations to spatial thinking in adolescence. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41235-020-00239-0
title: Bidirectional developmental model of spatial activities and spatial thinking across childhood and adolescence
description: The article proposes that relations between spatial activity participation and spatial thinking are bidirectional and can be examined at a single time point or across development (Fig. 1a, 1b). As the authors state, "participation in spatial activities may improve spatial thinking skills and strategies, and individuals with a greater capacity for spatial thinking may seek out opportunities to engage in spatial activities." The model distinguishes spatial skills from spatial habits of mind as distinct yet correlated facets of spatial thinking, and maps paths linking childhood activity participation, adolescent activity participation, and each facet. The present study tested the paths across development (Fig. 1b) rather than at a single point in time.
requirements: Measures of spatial activity participation at multiple developmental points (here, retrospective childhood CAQ and adolescent SAQ reports) and measures of both spatial skills and spatial habits of mind
constraints: The study was cross-sectional with retrospective self-report, so directionality of the relations could not be established; the authors call for longitudinal and intervention designs to test causal mechanisms
target_learners: Children and adolescents in STEM education contexts
target_learning_goals: Spatial thinking skills
Spatial habits of mind (spatial problem-solving strategies)
examples: The study regressed Paper Folding and SHOMI jointly on childhood and adolescent activity measures, testing paths B and C of the developmental model

Spatial activity participation in childhood and adolescence: consistency and relations to spatial thinking in adolescence. article_title: Dynamics of Teacher–Student Relationships: Stability and Change Across Elementary School and the Influence on Children’s Academic Success
citation: Spilt, J. L., Hughes, J. N., Wu, J.-Y., & Kwok, O.-M. (2012). Dynamics of Teacher-Student Relationships: Stability and Change across Elementary School and the Influence on Children's Academic Success. Child Development, 83(4), 1180-1195. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2012.01761.x
title: Bioecological and chronic-stress framing of teacher-student relationships as proximal processes whose cumulative exposure shapes development
description: The article applies the bioecological model (Bronfenbrenner & Morris, 2006), which posits four properties of development: "process, person, contexts, and time." Teacher-student interactions are proximal processes whose power depends on person, context, and time, and processes that recur over broader time intervals have greater impact than episodic ones. Combined with chronic stress models from peer-rejection research, this framing motivates modeling cumulative relationship trajectories rather than single-year snapshots, and interpreting chronic conflict's association with underachievement as an effect of prolonged relational adversity.
requirements: Longitudinal repeated measures of relationship quality across multiple years to capture cumulative exposure rather than single-time-point assessments
constraints: The article notes effects of a given process may differ across developmental periods, with long-term TSRQ effects possibly stronger in early school years than later years
target_learning_goals: academic achievement growth
school adjustment
examples: The study modeled grades 1-5 trajectories of conflict and warmth and tested their prediction of grade 6 achievement in 657 at-risk children

article_title: Constructing knowledge in the context of BioWorld
citation: Lajoie, S. P., Lavigne, N. C., Guerrera, C., & Munsie, S. D. (2001). Constructing knowledge in the context of BioWorld. Instructional Science, 29(2), 155-186. http://www.jstor.org/stable/41953546
title: BioWorld computer learning environment for high school biology
description: BioWorld is a computer learning environment for high school biology students that complements the curriculum with a hospital simulation where students diagnose diseases. It embeds five features: "patient scenario, on-line library, patient chart, evidence palette, and argumentation palette", which "provide users with different learning opportunities". Students hypothesize, collect evidence to confirm or disconfirm diagnoses, adjust a belief meter, and compare their final argument to an expert argument.
requirements: A set of patient scenario problems aligned with the biology curriculum, developed with the classroom teacher
Expert benchmarks of competent performance, established by physicians and teachers, against which student actions are compared
constraints: The intent is not to make physicians out of students, but to provide opportunities to reason scientifically about data in a simulated setting
target_learning_goals: scientific reasoning and argumentation about diseases
declarative knowledge of diseases and diagnostic procedural skill
examples: Four digestion patient scenarios (ciliacs, shigellosis, hepatitis A, cirrhosis) were solved by 20 grade-9 groups over a three-day period, each problem taking 20-45 minutes
key_sources: Lajoie, S. P., Lavigne, N. C., Guerrera, C., & Munsie, S. D. (2001). Constructing knowledge in the context of BioWorld. Instructional Science, 29(2), 155-186. http://www.jstor.org/stable/41953546

article_title: Constructing knowledge in the context of BioWorld
citation: Lajoie, S. P., Lavigne, N. C., Guerrera, C., & Munsie, S. D. (2001). Constructing knowledge in the context of BioWorld. Instructional Science, 29(2), 155-186. http://www.jstor.org/stable/41953546
title: Belief meter and evidence palette as memory and metacognitive scaffolds
description: The article accounts for BioWorld's support of scientific reasoning through tools that scaffold memory and metacognition. The evidence palette dynamically displays actions such as evidence selection, library searches and tests, and "Making actions and results visible in the evidence palette facilitates reasoning by supporting memory". The belief meter and evidence palette "support metacognition by providing reflection tools for learners that encourage them to assess their overall problem solving process rather than focus on a single action", externalizing and evaluating reasoning against expert arguments.
requirements: Actions and results must be made visible dynamically so learners can inspect prior plans and check how systematically they reviewed evidence
constraints: Metacognitive scaffolding in BioWorld targets the externalization and evaluation of reasoning during diagnosis, not other metacognitive activities
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness and self-evaluation during scientific problem solving
argumentation and evidence evaluation
examples: Students sort and categorize evidence, compare it to an expert argument, and receive a sequenced list of relevant information plus a narrated recap of how a physician solved the problem

article_title: Constructive alignment of a mathematics methodology module
citation: Spangenberg, E. D. (2025). Constructive alignment of a mathematics methodology module. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09712-z
title: Design teaching-and-learning activities from a bilateral perspective, considering learning outcomes and assessment tasks from both sides
description: Activities should be the mediating agency that merges learning outcomes with assessment tasks, informed by outcomes and also affecting tasks. The article illustrates misalignment: an initial activity asking for a reflection on 21st-century knowledge focused on theoretical content knowledge while the outcome required integrating functioning knowledge, so "teacher educators should follow a bilateral perspective (Biggs & Tang, 2011) by considering LOs and ATs from both sides in their design of TLAs". This ensures alignment of theory with practice and attends to what pre-service teachers are expected to achieve.
requirements: Outcomes specifying declarative or functioning knowledge so activities can target the right kind of knowledge
constraints: A misaligned activity steers learners toward theoretical content when the outcome demands functioning knowledge in practice
target_learning_goals: aligning activities with outcomes requiring functioning knowledge
becoming competent mathematics teachers
examples: A reflection-writing activity on 21st-century knowledge was replaced in principle by a GeoGebra-based activity developing an assessment to integrate into a mathematics lesson, better matching the integrating outcome
key_sources: Spangenberg, E. D. (2025). Constructive alignment of a mathematics methodology module. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09712-z

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Teacher Personality on Teacher Effectiveness and Burnout
citation: Lisa E. Kim, Verena Jörg & Robert M. Klassen. (2019). A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Teacher Personality on Teacher Effectiveness and Burnout. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9458-2
title: Big Five framework as the organizing taxonomy for teacher personality research
description: The article adopts the Big Five as the dominant personality framework, underpinned by the lexical hypothesis, and organizes its meta-analysis around five replicated domains: "openness(creative, curious, cultured), conscientiousness (organized, responsible, reliable), extraversion (sociable, assertive, energetic), agreeableness (kind, cooperative, trustful), and emotional stability (calm, secure, unemotional)". It treats the closely similar five-factor model (FFM) as combinable with Big Five domains, as prior meta-analyses do, and argues teacher personality research should use such established frameworks rather than ad hoc trait lists.
requirements: Personality measures used must be classifiable within the Big Five framework empirically or theoretically, as the article's own exclusion criteria state
constraints: The Big Five and FFM differ slightly, e.g., the FFM's broader definition of openness including unconventionality and behavioral flexibility
target_learners: teachers across elementary, secondary, and tertiary education
target_learning_goals: understanding which teacher personal characteristics relate to teacher effectiveness and burnout
examples: The meta-analysis classified 25 studies' personality measures (e.g., BFI, NEO-PI-R, 16PF) into Big Five domains and pooled their correlations with effectiveness and burnout
key_sources: Lisa E. Kim, Verena Jörg & Robert M. Klassen. (2019). A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Teacher Personality on Teacher Effectiveness and Burnout. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9458-2

article_title: A Motivational Perspective on (Anticipated) Mental Effort Investment: The Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat
citation: Tamara van Gog, Eva Janssen, Florence Lucas, Maaike Taheij (2024). A Motivational Perspective on (Anticipated) Mental Effort Investment: The Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat. Educational Psychology Review (2024) 36:54. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09861-6
title: The biopsychosocial model of challenge and threat explains motivational antecedents of (anticipated) mental effort investment
description: The biopsychosocial model of challenge and threat (Blascovich, 2008) describes how challenge and threat motivational states arise in goal-relevant motivated performance situations. As the article states, "These resource/demand evaluations result in a challenge motivational state when the evaluation of resources matches or exceeds the evaluation of demands, and in a threat motivational state when demands outweigh resources". The authors propose it as a lens for cognitive load theory to explain why, in similar instructional conditions, some students invest effort while others do not, and they test it in four feedback-valence experiments.
requirements: A motivated performance situation: a goal-relevant situation requiring instrumental cognitive responses, leading to task engagement
Measurement of challenge and threat states, via self-reports or physiological measures
constraints: The model was, at the time of writing, not yet widely applied in educational research
target_learning_goals: understanding and explaining individual differences in mental effort investment
examples: Four experiments manipulated predominantly positive vs. negative (and no) feedback on CRT or weekday problems and measured challenge/threat, self-efficacy, and effort ratings
key_sources: Tamara van Gog, Eva Janssen, Florence Lucas, Maaike Taheij (2024). A Motivational Perspective on (Anticipated) Mental Effort Investment: The Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat. Educational Psychology Review (2024) 36:54. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09861-6

article_title: Exploration of domains of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education research
citation: Fagerlund, J., Palsa, L., & Mertala, P. (2025). Exploration of domains of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education research. Educational Research Review, 46, Article 100663. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100663
title: Biesta's three domains of educational purpose (qualification, socialization, subjectification) as an organizing framework for data literacy education
description: The review applies Gert Biesta's (2009) account of "good education" to K-12 data literacy education, treating education as impacting three interconnected domains: qualification (equipping individuals with knowledge, skills, and dispositions), socialization (becoming part of social orders), and subjectification (becoming the subject of one's own life). The framework is used deductively to code 611 purpose expressions and inductively to map themes and their intersections. The review states the domains are "unique but also interconnected, and the effectiveness of education lies in how they intersect".
requirements: Purpose expressions in source literature must be sufficiently clear to code against the three domains; the review accepted only sufficiently clear arguments regarding educational purposes
constraints: The framework does not provide clear themes usable with minimal interpretation when operationalized in a new domain, which the authors say justified consensus-building coding
Conflicts between domains are possible; subjectification is described as the opposite of socialization in encouraging non-conformity
target_learning_goals: Data literacy education purposes spanning skills, social integration, and self-determination in data-rich contexts
examples: The review coded 611 expressions from 77 studies against the three domains and their intersecting areas, producing themes such as data competencies under qualification
key_sources: Fagerlund, J., Palsa, L., & Mertala, P. (2025). Exploration of domains of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education research. Educational Research Review, 46, Article 100663. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100663

article_title: Cubic Relations of Autonomous and Controlled Motivation to Achievement: A Cross-National Validation of Self-Determination Theory Using Response Surface Analysis
citation: Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cubic Relations of Autonomous and Controlled Motivation to Achievement: A Cross-National Validation of Self-Determination Theory Using Response Surface Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 36 (3). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09905-x
title: Bidimensional (circumplex) approach to SDT's motivational regulations, projecting the six regulation types onto combined autonomous and controlled motivation dimensions
description: The article advances a bidimensional projection of SDT's taxonomy in which the six motivational regulations are expressed as combined levels of autonomous motivation (AM) and controlled motivation (CM). It argues that "autonomous and controlled motivations may co-exist or exist independently from one another", so students may feel both, only one, or neither (non-regulation/amotivation). This circumplex approach integrates internal, external, introjected, identified, integrated regulation and non-regulation in one two-dimensional spectrum used to model achievement via cubic response surfaces.
requirements: Measures of autonomous and controlled motivation must be commensurate (standardized) so parametric constraints defining polynomial families are structurally valid.
constraints: The unidimensional simplex approach is reported not to fit data for specific disciplines and to contradict findings that AM and CM indicators correlate positively or non-significantly.
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement
Motivational regulation in school learning
examples: The study operationalizes AM via the Students Like Learning Mathematics scale and CM via the Students Value Mathematics scale in TIMSS 2019, then relates the two dimensions to achievement with cubic polynomial regression.
key_sources: Núñez-Regueiro, F. (2024). Cubic Relations of Autonomous and Controlled Motivation to Achievement: A Cross-National Validation of Self-Determination Theory Using Response Surface Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 36 (3). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09905-x

article_title: Tracing and Pointing Support Multimedia Learning: A Cross-Cultural Replication
citation: Yining Wang, Kexin Han, Paul Ginns. (2025). Tracing and Pointing Support Multimedia Learning: A Cross-Cultural Replication. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10005-7
title: Biologically primary tracing and pointing actions support acquisition of biologically secondary knowledge (cognitive load theory evolutionary account)
description: Within cognitive load theory's evolutionary framing, knowledge is split into biologically primary knowledge, acquired effortlessly without explicit instruction, and biologically secondary knowledge, which requires extensive working memory investment. The article contends touch-based pointing and tracing with the index finger are biologically primary actions that "can potentially enhance the learning process because they support learning-related processing without overly taxing working memory", reducing extraneous load by directing attention between text and diagrams. The present study tests this account cross-culturally by instructing Chinese-speaking adults to trace and point while learning heart anatomy.
requirements: Pre-lesson instructions directing learners to make touch-based pointing and tracing actions linking text and diagram elements
constraints: Effects on intrinsic load and intrinsic motivation were not supported in this study; the attention-direction (extraneous load) account is the one the authors treat as supported
target_learners: adult university students learning biologically secondary knowledge such as anatomy
target_learning_goals: comprehension of multimedia lesson material combining expository text and diagrams
examples: Participants were instructed to point at words and corresponding diagram locations, leave a finger on the diagram, and trace along arrows indicating blood flow during a 25-minute paper-based lesson
key_sources: Yining Wang, Kexin Han, Paul Ginns. (2025). Tracing and Pointing Support Multimedia Learning: A Cross-Cultural Replication. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10005-7

article_title: Examining the Effects of Family-Implemented Literacy Interventions for School-Aged Children: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Dahl-Leonard, K., Hall, C., Cho, E., Capin, P., Roberts, G. J., Kehoe, K. F., Haring, C., Peacott, D., & Demchak, A. (2025). Examining the Effects of Family-Implemented Literacy Interventions for School-Aged Children: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09985-3
title: Bioecological systems framework: home-based family literacy interactions as proximal processes in the microsystem
description: The article frames family-implemented literacy interventions using Bronfenbrenner's bioecological systems framework, in which context comprises five interrelated systems (microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem, macrosystem, chronosystem). Home experiences influence children's learning at the same level as school experiences because both sit in the microsystem, the system most proximal to the child. In the discussion, the authors describe interactions between a child and a family member in home-based literacy interventions as "proximal processes, occurring at the level of the microsystem", which Bronfenbrenner called "the primary engines of development". The framework motivates the meta-analysis's premise that families can improve both code-related and meaning-related skills supporting reading comprehension.
requirements: Interventions must be implemented by a family member or caregiver in the home, as proximal processes arise from reciprocal interactions within the microsystem.
target_learners: School-aged children in grades K-12, including students with or at risk for reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Code-focused literacy skills (phonological awareness, decoding/word reading, spelling, text reading)
Meaning-focused literacy skills (vocabulary, listening comprehension, reading comprehension)
examples: The meta-analysis included 25 interventions across 22 studies in which parents or primary caregivers delivered literacy activities such as paired reading, dialogic reading, repeated reading, and interactive homework at home.
key_sources: Dahl-Leonard, K., Hall, C., Cho, E., Capin, P., Roberts, G. J., Kehoe, K. F., Haring, C., Peacott, D., & Demchak, A. (2025). Examining the Effects of Family-Implemented Literacy Interventions for School-Aged Children: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09985-3

article_title: How Personality Matters for Education Research
citation: Hayley K. Jach, Lisa Bardach, Kou Murayama. (2023). How Personality Matters for Education Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09807-4
title: Big Five trait framework: traits as continuous, hierarchical, context-dependent dimensions
description: The review frames personality traits as "characteristic patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviours manifest in isomorphic situations", organised hierarchically with facets below broad Big Five dimensions. Traits are continuous dimensions, not types: trait scores correspond to the average of density distributions of momentary states, and expression is context-dependent. The framework serves as a shared nomenclature that reduces redundancy and locates narrower traits such as grit within conscientiousness.
requirements: High-quality measurement with established scales (e.g. BFI-2) to reflect target constructs accurately
constraints: Most factor-structure research was performed in WEIRD nations; a cited systematic review found little support for stricter forms of measurement invariance across cultures
target_learners: students across primary, secondary, and tertiary education
target_learning_goals: predicting and supporting academic performance, motivation, engagement, and wellbeing
examples: The review uses the Big Five to organise discussion of predictors, interventions, personalised learning, and outcome measurement throughout
key_sources: Hayley K. Jach, Lisa Bardach, Kou Murayama. (2023). How Personality Matters for Education Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09807-4

article_title: How Personality Matters for Education Research
citation: Hayley K. Jach, Lisa Bardach, Kou Murayama. (2023). How Personality Matters for Education Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09807-4
title: Table 1 overview of current Big Five personality scales with the BFI-2 recommended for education research
description: Table 1 of the review lists the most popular current personality trait scales with item counts, facets per trait, and open-access status, spanning medium-length scales (BFI-2, BFI-2-Short, Big Five Aspect Scales, NEO-FFI, HEXACO, BFI), large scales (IPIP-NEO, NEO-PI-R), and super-short scales (Ten Item Personality Inventory, BFI-2-Extra-Short, Mini-IPIP). The review recommends the BFI-2 for its breadth without compromising efficiency.
requirements: Researchers should match scale length and facet coverage to survey space and the specificity of the target outcome, using narrow measures when the bandwidth/fidelity trade-off favours them
constraints: Super-short scales are "recommended only when brevity is essential"; the NEO-FFI and NEO-PI-R are not open access
target_learners: students in education research studies at any level
target_learning_goals: measuring personality traits as predictors, personalisation dimensions, or outcome measures in educational studies
examples: The review recommends including a global Big Five measure alongside narrow scales when survey space allows, to enable cross-study comparison and meta-analysis

article_title: An Evolutionary Approach to Motivation and Learning: Differentiating Biologically Primary and Secondary Knowledge
citation: Kate M. Xu, Sarah Coertjens, Florence Lespiau, Kim Ouwehand, Hanke Korpershoek, Fred Paas, David C. Geary. (2024). An Evolutionary Approach to Motivation and Learning: Differentiating Biologically Primary and Secondary Knowledge. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09880-3
title: Evolutionary framework distinguishing biologically primary from biologically secondary knowledge and motivation
description: The article builds on Geary's framework distinguishing "biologically secondary knowledge and skills learned in schools from those acquired nearly automatically during development (e.g., language, face recognition)". Primary knowledge emerges through built-in cognitive and motivational scaffolds organized as folk psychology, folk biology, and folk physics; secondary domains such as physics and mathematics lack these biases, "require more explicit, organized instruction", and their evolutionary novelty explains declining motivation during schooling. The study tests this framework empirically with a vocabulary task.
requirements: Distinguishing content by evolutionary relevance of the knowledge being learned
constraints: The built-in cognitive and motivational biases do not extend to most academic domains
target_learners: school and university students learning academic content
target_learning_goals: academic knowledge and skills in evolutionarily novel domains such as mathematics, physics, and reading
examples: The study embedded primary (e.g., mother, love) and secondary (e.g., computer, gravity) concepts in Dutch-fictional word pairs and contrasted recall, motivation, and cognitive load between the two knowledge types.
key_sources: Kate M. Xu, Sarah Coertjens, Florence Lespiau, Kim Ouwehand, Hanke Korpershoek, Fred Paas, David C. Geary. (2024). citation: Chen, Ouhao. (2016). The Worked Example Effect, the Generation Effect, and Element Interactivity. PhD thesis, School of Education, UNSW. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/55865
title: Biologically primary versus biologically secondary knowledge distinction
description: Drawing on Geary's theory, the thesis distinguishes two knowledge categories relevant to instructional design: "Biologically primary knowledge is learnable but not teachable, whereas biologically secondary knowledge is learnable as well as teachable." Primary knowledge, such as speaking one's mother language or general problem-solving strategies like means-ends analysis, is acquired naturally and effortlessly without explicit instruction. Secondary knowledge, such as writing, is culture-specific, effortful and conscious, and requires formal instruction — so the design of its teaching matters. An informal test is whether acquisition requires instructional supports.

target_learning_goals: distinguishing knowledge that needs explicit teaching from knowledge acquired automatically

title: Bivariate latent change score modeling as a method for testing dynamic co-development of two constructs
description: The article's methodological framework combines cross-lagged panel and parallel-process growth modeling. "Bivariate latent change score (LCS) models make use of longitudinal data to define the nature of dynamic relations between two variables over time," with change decomposed into a constant change component (α ∗ η), a proportional autoregressive component (β), and a cross-lagged component (γ) that "estimates whether one construct is a leading indicator of change in the second construct." title: Biologically based neural circuit modelling as a multi-level framework integrating biological information to study fear and anxiety networks
description: The review advocates biologically based computational modelling as a framework for understanding fear/anxiety networks, arguing these are complex dynamical systems that defy intuition. The authors state that "biologically based modelling can be used to integrate biological information at different levels of organisation", allowing study of emergent properties and rapid quantitative testing of hypotheses difficult to address experimentally. The framework spans neuronal (Hodgkin–Huxley ionic channels), synaptic (reversal potential, rise/decay times, facilitation/depression, plasticity), and network levels, and envisions "a reciprocal interaction" between models and experiments in which observations constrain models and verify predictions.

Output measures such as the magnitude of neuronal responses to the CS as a proxy for the intensity of emotional responses.
constraints: Output measures used so far "will not sufﬁce when studying more complex and realistic behavioural paradigms" beyond classical fear conditioning.
The paper focuses on the synaptic, cellular and systems levels, leaving molecular-level and cognitive-level modelling to other reviews.
Network models typically cannot incorporate all cell types and compensate by adjusting proportions and synaptic strengths.

target_learning_goals: Understanding neural circuit mechanisms of fear learning and extinction
Linking circuit dysfunction to maladaptive fear responses in mental disorders

description: A biophysically realistic computational model of the lateral amygdala described in the review. The number of LA neurons was scaled down 30 to 1, "including 800 principal cells and 200 fast-spiking interneurons", distributed randomly in a realistic tri-dimensional representation of the horn-shaped LAd. citation: Pérez-Sanagustín, M., Muñoz-Merino, P. J., Alario-Hoyos, C., Soldani, X., & Delgado Kloos, C. (2015). Lessons Learned from the Design of Situated Learning Environments to Support Collaborative Knowledge Construction. Computers & Education, 87, 70-82. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.03.019
title: Bidirectional SLE built on etiquetAR bidirectional QR codes
description: An indoor situated learning environment in which each industrial machine carries a "bidirectional" QR code generated with etiquetAR, an authoring tool whose tags "provide information (as do tradition al QR codes )" but "also collect user -generated content". Each code links to a machine video, an image of main components, and a question; answers left by teams become visible to anyone scanning later, opening a cross-team collaboration channel. Students answer via their own smartphones or teacher-provided tablets, then peer-evaluate classmates' answers.
requirements: Mobile devices (students' smartphones or teacher-provided tablets) with QR readers
A reliable technological setting with adequate Internet connectivity for loading videos
constraints: Teachers reported the SLE "is not  designed to operate in settings with slow or limited Internet connectivity"
Answers are removed after each session, so teams see only answers from their own laboratory session
target_learners: post-secondary mechanical engineering students in laboratory sessions
target_learning_goals: knowledge of machine pieces, functionality and usage
collaborative knowledge construction and reflection on peer answers
examples: In the lab session, a bidirectional QR code was attached to each of five machines (Hydraulic Press, Punch Press, Numerical Control Lathe, Machining Center, Vertical Drilling Machine)
key_sources: Pérez-Sanagustín, M., Muñoz-Merino, P. J., Alario-Hoyos, C., Soldani, X., & Delgado Kloos, C. (2015). Lessons Learned from the Design of Situated Learning Environments to Support Collaborative Knowledge Construction. Computers & Education, 87, 70-82. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.03.019

article_title: Lessons learned from the design of situated learning environments to support collaborative knowledge construction
citation: Pérez-Sanagustín, M., Muñoz-Merino, P. J., Alario-Hoyos, C., Soldani, X., & Delgado Kloos, C. (2015). Lessons Learned from the Design of Situated Learning Environments to Support Collaborative Knowledge Construction. Computers & Education, 87, 70-82. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.03.019
title: Design indoor SLEs for collaborative knowledge construction using bidirectional tags and open questions
description: From the cross-analysis of quantitative results and teacher opinions, the article derives lessons for designing SLEs that support collaborative knowledge construction indoors. Its core recommendation is that "providing a technological setting based on  bidirectional tags and learning activities based on open questions is recommendable for teachers" who want such SLEs, because open questions better support the exchange of different perspectives and bidirectional tags enable cross-team collaboration and awareness of the collaborative process.
requirements: Reliable technology that does not interfere with the learning process
Open (higher-order) questions rather than closed ones
A script to organize teamwork at each machine
Activities that explicitly push students to reflect on and evaluate classmates' answers
constraints: Teachers observed that "Sometimes students accept erroneous answers from others; they do not reflect on others' answers  enough", so the collaboration channel alone is insufficient for reflection
Slow or limited Internet connectivity hampers the design
target_learners: post-secondary students in lab sessions and similar indoor authentic settings
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction
higher-order thinking such as analysis and evaluation
examples: The article's lesson (4) grounds the recommendation in the validation of H1, H2 and H3; lesson (6) calls for exercises that inspire students to better evaluate peer answers; lesson (9) recommends technology allowing teachers to monitor activity and assess in real time

article_title: An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS
citation: Angelides, M. C. & Agius, H. W. (2001). An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS. https://www.brunel.ac.uk/~cssthwa/
title: Bigger Bits: interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI
description: Bigger Bits is an interactive multimedia learning environment built with COSMOS that teaches VLSI within the context of a fictitious computer electronics manufacturer called Bigger Bits Ltd. It uses an intelligent tutoring system architecture with domain, remedial, tutoring and student knowledge, with COSMOS forming the domain knowledge and SEMs forming the basis of the rest of the architecture. Domain knowledge was based on textbooks and advanced handbooks, with media drawn from educational videos, promotional videos and specially filmed footage.
requirements: COSMOS as the domain knowledge component
target_learning_goals: application of theoretical knowledge of VLSI product and process

article_title: The Effectiveness of Feedback for L1-English and L2-Writing Development: A Meta-Analysis. TOEFL iBT™ Research Report. TOEFL iBT-14. ETS RR-11-05
citation: Douglas Biber, Tatiana Nekrasova, and Brad Horn. (2011). The Effectiveness of Feedback for L1-English and L2-Writing Development: A Meta-Analysis. ETS Research Report RR-11-05. https://www.ets.org/toefl
title: A 16-variable coding rubric characterizing feedback by source, mode, focus, type, and tone, plus outcome measures
description: The report develops an explicit coding rubric that itemizes all important factors varying across feedback studies, developed inductively by reading a wide sample of studies. It includes 16 variables covering research paradigm, design type, target language and population, writing-task genre and length, and five feedback dimensions — the article states that "feedback can be described with respect to five variables: type, focus, tone, mode, and source" — plus outcome measures. The rubric was applied to categorize all studies in the 306-article corpus and to code the subset entering the statistical meta-analysis, providing the basis for subsequent effect-size comparison.
requirements: Studies must be codable on all rubric variables, with values such as teacher/peer/tutor/self/computer for source and oral/written/computer-mediated for mode
constraints: Proficiency level applies to L2 studies only; some variables such as tone were unreported in most studies
Qualitative studies cannot be included in a quantitative meta-analysis
target_learners: L1-English and L2-English writing students from K-12 through graduate levels
target_learning_goals: Writing proficiency development, including grammatical accuracy, holistic quality, revision behavior, and attitudes toward feedback
examples: Table 1 itemizes variables and values, e.g., type of feedback coded as location of error, comment, direct correction, editing codes, and multiple types

article_title: Psychosocial factors associated with academic performance in medical students: a systematic review.
citation: Ríos Andrade Raúl, Peralta Ramírez Aziel Alejandro, Trujillo López Sergio. (2026). Psychosocial factors associated with academic performance in medical students: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08742-6
title: Biopsychosocial four-domain framework of psychosocial factors in medical student academic performance
description: The review organizes psychosocial factors using the biopsychosocial model originally proposed by Engel (1977), integrating psychological, social, and contextual dimensions relevant to medical education. It categorizes factors into four domains: affective symptoms (stress, anxiety, depression, distress, burnout); motivation and learning attitudes (intrinsic/extrinsic motivation, engagement, study habits); personality and trait-like characteristics (emotional intelligence, grit, resilience, coping styles); and social and environmental factors (perceived social support, socioeconomic disadvantage, learning environment, institutional climate). The framework frames academic achievement as resulting from "dynamic interactions between individual psychological functioning, social resources, and contextual demands."
requirements: Only studies evaluating one or more of these four domains in relation to academic performance were considered eligible.
constraints: The review states the predominance of cross-sectional designs and varied measurement tools precludes causal inference.
target_learning_goals: academic performance (GPA, examinations, licensing or OSCE scores)
key_sources: Ríos Andrade Raúl, Peralta Ramírez Aziel Alejandro, Trujillo López Sergio. (2026). Psychosocial factors associated with academic performance in medical students: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08742-6

article_title: Doctors' and Pharmacists' knowledge, skills, and perception of mental frailty in older adults: a scoping review.
citation: Bregar Branko, Vatovec Katarina, Ferlan Istinič Marjeta, Mikolič Brence Petra, Oreški Suzana, Vinko Matej, Bertole Tjaša. (2026). Doctors' and Pharmacists' knowledge, skills, and perception of mental frailty in older adults: a scoping review. BMC Primary Care. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-026-03300-x
title: Biopsychosocial model integration as the framework for recognizing and managing mental frailty in primary care
description: The review organizes its findings around the biopsychosocial model, in which physical, cognitive, psychological, and social vulnerability in older adults are intertwined and should not be considered in isolation. It concludes that "Systematic training of healthcare professionals and consistent integration of the biopsychosocial model are crucial to improve recognition and management of mental frailty in older adults." The framework underpins the review's recommendation that education address the mental dimension of frailty, not only its physical aspect.
requirements: Systematic training of healthcare professionals so the mental dimension of frailty is addressed alongside physical and social dimensions
constraints: The review states it does not establish causal relationships or evaluate intervention effectiveness
target_learning_goals: Recognize mental frailty in older adults
Apply holistic, interdisciplinary assessment and management of frailty
examples: The review's thematic analysis treats frailty as multidimensional, noting frail individuals are more often burdened with chronic diseases, polypharmacotherapy, falls, depressive symptoms, sarcopenia, and cognitive impairment
key_sources: Bregar Branko, Vatovec Katarina, Ferlan Istinič Marjeta, Mikolič Brence Petra, Oreški Suzana, Vinko Matej, Bertole Tjaša. (2026). article_title: Cumulative Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) and School Outcomes During Adolescence: A Scoping Review.
citation: Stoddard, S. A., Moore, C. R., Polick, C. S., & Moss, J. M. (2026). Cumulative Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) and School Outcomes During Adolescence: A Scoping Review. The Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.70209
title: Biopsychosocial pathway framework linking cumulative ACE exposure to adolescent school outcomes
description: The review organizes mediational evidence through a biopsychosocial model in which cumulative ACE exposure may influence school outcomes through biopsychosocial, mental/behavioral health, and more proximal school processes. Repeated or chronic adversity may lead to toxic stress, disrupting executive functioning, emotion regulation, and other learning processes, which are then associated with behavioral health, engagement, attendance, achievement, and classroom functioning, ultimately relating to high school completion. The framework is illustrated in the review's Figure 2.
requirements: Longitudinal designs are recommended to test pathways from ACEs, distinct behavioral health symptoms, school engagement, disciplinary experiences, academic performance, and educational attainment
constraints: The review notes current mediational evidence is preliminary and that additional research on mediating pathways, protective factors, and at-risk subpopulations is a critical first step
target_learners: US adolescents aged 12-18 exposed to cumulative adverse childhood experiences
target_learning_goals: Improved school engagement, attendance, academic achievement, and high school completion
examples: The review's Figure 2 diagrams pathways linking cumulative ACE exposure to adolescent school outcomes through biopsychosocial, mental/behavioral health, and proximal school processes

article_title: Clinical skills development for healthcare practitioners working with patients with persistent physical symptoms (PPS) in healthcare settings: a systematic review and narrative synthesis.
citation: Thursby Stacie, Dismore Lorelle, Swainston Katherine. (2024). Clinical skills development for healthcare practitioners working with patients with persistent physical symptoms (PPS) in healthcare settings: a systematic review and narrative synthesis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05306-4
title: Use the biopsychosocial model as the theoretical framework for PPS training programmes and holistic consultations
description: The review recommends educators utilise the biopsychosocial model, "endorsed by several of the included studies", as a theoretical framework for developing training that addresses the multifaceted presentation of PPS. It supports moving away from the biomedical model, breaking mind–body dualism, and structuring consultations around biological, psychological and social domains so patients take agency in their own care.
requirements: Training must be clearly intended to develop psychologically informed practice working holistically at the interface of somatic and psychological care
constraints: The review reports a gap in existing programmes around explanations of psychosocial and physiological interrelating factors, and that only one included study used a tool facilitating a structured consultation
target_learners: healthcare practitioners in primary and secondary care
target_learning_goals: holistic assessment, treatment and management of PPS
making the link between symptoms and psychosocial stressors
patient self-management and agency
examples: Two included studies (Weiland et al.; Schaefert et al.) drew on the biopsychosocial model to inform a holistic approach within consultations

Clinical skills development for healthcare practitioners working with patients with persistent physical symptoms (PPS) in healthcare settings: a systematic review and narrative synthesis. article_title: Systematic reviews, systematic error and the acquisition of clinical knowledge.
citation: Mickenautsch Steffen. (2010). Systematic reviews, systematic error and the acquisition of clinical knowledge. BMC Medical Research Methodology. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-10-53
title: Include bias-controlling measures in clinical trial study designs
description: The article argues that empirical evidence on systematic error justifies including bias-controlling measures in clinical trial design. It states that "inclusion of bias-controlling measures; such as randomization, blinding and attrition control, into the study design of clinical trials is justified". These measures respectively address selection, performance/detection, and attrition bias, limiting over-estimation of treatment effects.
requirements: Randomization (random sequence allocation and allocation concealment), blinding, and intention-to-treat analysis must be applied to address each bias type
constraints: Trials investigating subjective outcome measures are especially at risk of over-estimation
target_learning_goals: designing clinical trials that limit systematic error and protect internal validity
examples: The article cites meta-epidemiological evidence that over-estimation from attrition bias can reach up to 25% and from inadequate randomization and blinding may reach above 50%
key_sources: Mickenautsch Steffen. (2010). Systematic reviews, systematic error and the acquisition of clinical knowledge. BMC Medical Research Methodology. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-10-53

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of LLM Effects on Students across Qualification, Socialisation, and Subjectification
citation: Jiayu Huang, Ruoxin Ritter Wang, Jen-Hao Liu, Boming Xia, Yue Huang, Ruoxi Sun, Jason (Minhui) Xue, Jinan Zou. (2025). A Meta-Analysis of LLM Effects on Students Across Qualification, Socialisation, and Subjectification. A PREPRINT. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22725
title: Biesta's tripartite framework of educational purposes (qualification, socialisation, subjectification) as an evaluative lens for LLM interventions
description: The article organises all outcome classification and effect estimation through Biesta's account of education's three purposes. Qualification is "the acquisition of knowledge, skills, and dispositions"; socialisation is the induction of learners into social, cultural, and political communities; subjectification is "the formation of learners as autonomous and responsible beings". The framework treats the purposes as interdependent and often in tension, so the authors read outcomes at the level of purposes rather than collapsing them into a single effectiveness score, making design allocations of control and participation empirically visible.
requirements: Outcomes must be classified against the original studies' own definitions of their measures, via the article's two-step coding procedure, to stay faithful to context
constraints: The purposes are interdependent and often in tension; the article notes that designs emphasising answer provision can raise qualification metrics while dampening participation or autonomy
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students using student-facing LLM interventions
target_learning_goals: Knowledge and skill acquisition
social participation and collaboration
learner autonomy, agency, and identity
examples: The meta-analysis classified 188 effect sizes from 133 studies into the three purposes and estimated purpose-level effects and within-purpose moderators
key_sources: Jiayu Huang, Ruoxin Ritter Wang, Jen-Hao Liu, Boming Xia, Yue Huang, Ruoxi Sun, Jason (Minhui) Xue, Jinan Zou. (2025). A Meta-Analysis of LLM Effects on Students Across Qualification, Socialisation, and Subjectification. A PREPRINT. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22725

article_title: The Effect of Mobile Learning Applications on Students' Academic Achievement and Attitudes toward Mobile Learning
citation: Kadir DEMIR, Ercan AKPINAR. (2018). The effect of mobile learning applications on students' academic achievement and attitudes toward mobile learning. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology. http://dx.doi.org/10.17220/mojet.2018.04.004
title: Bite-sized, learner-centered mobile content design principles
description: The article describes mobile learning content design in which materials are built on mobile design principles rather than adapted e-learning objects. It states that "Mobile learning contents should be presented in small chunks instead of presenting the entire material", calling such chunks nuggets or bite-sized, and lists design guidelines including quick and simple interactions, flexible materials, and a learner-centered approach. In this study, bite-sized and interactive course content was created and used with native applications on tablet computers kept by students for 12 weeks.
requirements: Content designed on mobile design principles rather than adapted e-learning objects
Quick and simple interactions and flexible materials that can change according to learner needs
Learner-centered design of materials
constraints: Mobile learning cannot replace formal education but supports learning outside the classroom
target_learning_goals: course content learning in a graphic and animation course
examples: The researchers created bite-sized and interactive course content and provided native applications on tablet computers that students kept during the research
