article_title: Expediency of Study of the Scientists' Biographies in Physics Course
citation: Korsun, I. (2017). Expediency of Study of the Scientists' Biographies in Physics Course. International Journal of Instruction, 10(2), 229-244. http://www.e-iji.net/dosyalar/iji_2017_2_15.pdf
title: Select biographic material by curriculum connection, understandability, interest, humanization and national consciousness
description: The article adopts criteria for selecting historical and biographic material in physics teaching. As printed, "Golovko (2000) has identified criteria for the selection of historical material: (1) organic connectedness with the curriculum; (2) availability for understand;" and further criteria include promoting learning efficiency, interest in physics, humanization of education, and education of national consciousness. These criteria answer the problem that detailed biographies are often written for specialists and are complex for learners.
requirements: Material must be connected with the curriculum and understandable to learners, since much published biographical information is intended for specialists and historians of science
constraints: The criteria are attributed to Golovko (2000) and applied to school physics course material in Ukraine
target_learning_goals: understanding the evolution of science
formation of interest in physics
humanization of education
examples: The article's own method of studying scientists' biographies was built by applying these criteria to select educational material

article_title: Innovation in Early Math Education: The Whole Teacher Approach to Professional Development
citation: McCray, J. & Chen, J.-Q. (2013). Innovation in Early Math Education: The Whole Teacher Approach to Professional Development. title: Big Ideas in early mathematics as an organizing tool for teaching
description: Central to the PD program is teachers' understanding of Big Ideas in early mathematics and their use in classroom teaching. Big Ideas are defined as "clusters of concepts and skills that are mathematically central and coherent, consistent with children's thinking, and generative of future learning." article_title: The Effect of Using Facebook in Writing Education on Writing Achievement, Attitude, Anxiety and Self-Efficacy Perception
citation: Hatice Altunkaya, Ersoy Topuzkanamış. (2018). The Effect of Using Facebook in Writing Education on Writing Achievement, Attitude, Anxiety and Self-efficacy Perception. Universal Journal of Educational Research 6(10): 2133-2142. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2018.061010
title: Biggs and Moore learning process model as the intervention framework
description: The article structures its 14-week intervention around the learning process model developed by Biggs and Moore, which the authors describe as comprising "four basic components that influence the learning outcomes": a well-structured knowledge base, motivational content, interactions (teacher-student and student-student), and active learning. Facebook sharing and feedback were used to operationalize the interaction and motivation components within constructivist, process-based writing instruction.

Clear goals and instructions and a warm, positive climate created by the teacher
Teacher-student and student-student interactions
Active learning

target_learning_goals: written expression skills
writing achievement
examples: The book Written Expression with Weekly Activities provided the knowledge base; self-review, peer review and final publication steps were conducted in both groups for student-student and student-teacher interactions

citation: Sasikala, P., & Tanyong, S. (2016). A Study on Simulation Methods in Academic Success With Reference To Teaching Biology for Education Students. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(11). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105115
title: Biology Success Test (Pre-Test/Post-Test) instrument for measuring academic success in biology instruction.
description: The researchers prepared a multiple-choice success test about biology for daily life, used as both pre-test and post-test to measure academic success. The test included three sections: fill in the blanks (10 items), matching (10 items), and short answer (10 items). Validity and reliability were checked with 45 students outside the main study sample. The test measured "the percentage of correct answers in the test and the percentage of the item known."

Validity and reliability checked with a separate sample of 45 students
constraints: Designed specifically for the 'daily life and importance' biology unit

article_title: Understanding Impact Variation in Family Rewards: The Role of Schools and Neighborhoods on a Conditional Cash Transfer Program
citation: Wolf, S., Aber, J. L., & Morris, P. A. (2013). Understanding Impact Variation in Family Rewards: The Role of Schools and Neighborhoods on a Conditional Cash Transfer Program. SREE Spring 2013 Conference.
title: Ecological theory of human development as a framework for understanding setting-level moderation of program effects
description: The study is grounded in ecological theory (Bronfenbrenner & Morris, 2006), extending subgroup analysis from the individual level to the contextual level. It asks "what works best in which contexts?" by examining how "key school and neighborhood characteristics may have moderated the effects of Family Rewards." Setting-level moderators can exist at different levels, including family, economic context, locale, or prevalence of community services.
requirements: Program impact evaluation must include measures of the settings (schools, neighborhoods) in which participants are embedded, linked at the appropriate level.
constraints: The abstract proposes this framework but does not report completed moderator results.

Educational processes and motivation
Time use

article_title: Disentangling the dynamic directional associations between positive and negative risk-taking behaviors and academic development in adolescents: a four-wave longitudinal analysis.
citation: Wang Enna, Zhang Junjie. (2026). Disentangling the dynamic directional associations between positive and negative risk-taking behaviors and academic development in adolescents: a four-wave longitudinal analysis. BMC Psychology, 14, 1273. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-05248-0
title: Bipolar continuum model of adolescent risk-taking validated longitudinally in a non-Western context
description: The study applies the Duell and Steinberg framework conceptualizing risk-taking as "a bipolar continuum, with negative risk-taking behavior ... at one pole, and positive risk-taking behavior ... at the opposite pole". The four-wave findings provide what the authors call "systematic longitudinal validation of the bipolar continuum model of adolescent risk-taking" beyond Western contexts, showing valence-dependent, time-varying associations with academic development. The model holds that normative sensation seeking can be channeled into either facilitative or harmful risk-taking.
requirements: Longitudinal multi-wave designs are needed to document cumulative developmental benefits that short-term assessments miss
constraints: Validated among Chinese adolescents in a high-stakes educational context; generalizability to other cultural contexts is not established
target_learning_goals: academic engagement
academic achievement
adaptive risk-taking
key_sources: Wang Enna, Zhang Junjie. (2026). Disentangling the dynamic directional associations between positive and negative risk-taking behaviors and academic development in adolescents: a four-wave longitudinal analysis. BMC Psychology, 14, 1273. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-05248-0

article_title: Tailoring hybrid flipped learning course design: exploring motivation, personality, and experiences of students and faculty.
citation: Alshareef Ali M., Alhasani Mona, Qamar Nabeel, Alhazmi Aiman. (2026). Tailoring hybrid flipped learning course design: exploring motivation, personality, and experiences of students and faculty. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09570-4
title: Big Five personality traits as moderators of motivational experience in hybrid flipped learning
description: The article integrates the Big Five Factor Model with the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory to explain how individual differences shape engagement in hybrid flipped learning. It treats personality traits as moderators of motivational responses to course design: conscientiousness and agreeableness support positive motivation, extraversion and neuroticism create vulnerabilities, and openness eases adaptation. The Big Five provides "a standardized taxonomy that predicts variations in people's thoughts, feelings, behaviours, and actions," while the IMI, "developed within Self-Determination Theory," captures interest, competence, effort, tension, and value.
requirements: Validated self-report instruments for both personality and motivation dimensions
constraints: Associations are correlational from a cross-sectional design and cannot establish causality
target_learning_goals: intrinsic motivation in hybrid learning
adaptive course design
examples: PLS-SEM modeling of 149 student responses linked each Big Five trait to specific IMI subscales

title: Bioecological additive multiple-risk model of educational underachievement in students with ADHD and/or autism
description: The article applies Bronfenbrenner's bioecological systems theory, in which a child's academic development is shaped jointly by individual constitution and the family microsystem. Its findings support a version in which child NDD status and family factors act as "independent predictors of academic outcomes", i.e., risks that add rather than interact multiplicatively. This stands against differential-susceptibility accounts (Belsky) predicting stronger family effects among children with NDD. The authors frame it as "a multiple (biopsychosocial) risk model" viable for understanding achievement in all students.

target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting academic achievement (grades, upper-secondary eligibility) for students with neurodevelopmental disorders
examples: The study tested the model by fitting regression main effects and interaction terms for ADHD/autism, closeness, conflict, and parental education on grade scores and eligibility in 12,029 twins.

title: A four-factor bifactor model of executive functions in children
description: The article models executive functions as a bifactor structure in which all nine tasks load on a common factor, with additional specific factors for inhibition, working memory, and cognitive flexibility. As the article states, the common factor "represents what is common between the nine executive function tasks" while the subfactors capture "what is specific to each executive function construct." The model reached excellent fit (CFI = 0.980, TLI = 0.953, RMSEA = 0.041, SRMR = 0.031) and enabled extraction of factor scores for mediation analyses.

constraints: The common factor was not related to any school topic or to cardiorespiratory fitness, and interpreting what it represents remains challenging

description: A simulation training element in which fellows sew biotissues mimicking the pancreas and jejunum to practise the PJ anastomosis used in pancreaticoduodenectomy. Recorded drills reviewed by blinded graders

citation: AlShebli Bedoor, Makovi Kinga, Rahwan Talal. (2020). The association between early career informal mentorship in academic collaborations and junior author performance. Nature Communications. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-19723-8
title: Two-measure framework of informal mentorship quality: big-shot experience and hub experience
description: The article conceptualizes mentorship quality in scientific collaborations with two independent variables: big-shot experience, the mentors' average citations per annum before mentorship, which "captures how much of a 'big-shot' the mentors of the protégé are", and hub experience, the mentors' average degree in the collaboration network. The outcome is protégés' post-mentorship impact measured as c5 citations on papers written without mentors. The framework is applied via coarsened exact matching across millions of pairs.
requirements: Mentor–protégé pairs identified from coauthorship between junior (academic age ≤ 7) and senior scientists sharing discipline and US-based affiliation, with papers of 20 or fewer co-authors
constraints: The article states CEM "does not establish the existence of a causal effect"; the article was retracted in December 2020
target_learners: early-career scientists (junior researchers in their first 7 years)
target_learning_goals: career development and scientific impact of junior researchers through informal mentorship
examples: CEM comparisons of quintiles Qi+1 vs. Qi of each mentorship-quality measure across 3 million mentor–protégé pairs spanning ten disciplines

article_title: Factors affecting senior medical students' career choice.
citation: Querido Sophie, van den Broek Sjoukje, de Rond Marlies, Wigersma Lode, ten Cate Olle. (2018). Factors affecting senior medical students’ career choice. International Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.5c14.de75
title: Billett's workplace learning theory as an account of student agency in career choice
description: The article uses Billett's workplace learning theory to explain why students proactively gather career information: the workplace is "an implicit learning environment wherein the learner negotiates participation in work activities - and so the learning process - with those individuals representing the interests of the workplace". Students can use the affordances offered by the workplace in various ways, and student-initiated information collection is described as an explicit result of such agency, contributing to changes in their ways of knowing and sense of self.
requirements: An account of learning for work that acknowledges the independence of individuals acting within the interdependence of the social practice of work
target_learning_goals: career preference formation
agency in workplace learning
examples: Students contacting gynaecologists to shadow them for two days and ask questions about residency applications

title: Author-designed 24-item questionnaire on perceptions toward biostatistics in five sections
description: A 5-point Likert-type questionnaire developed by a design group of biostatistics educators, a psychologist and postgraduates, piloted with 90 first-year postgraduates. "The resulting questionnaire (Additional file 1) was structured with 24 items in five sections: (A) value, (B) comment, (C) expectation, (D) reform, and (E) ability." Reliability estimates were within the desired range with Cronbach's α 0.70–0.72, except the reform section (0.45).

Results cannot be compared with studies using standard scales such as SATS

examples: Piloted with 90 randomly selected first-year postgraduates to assess comprehension and face validity

title: Biotexture 3D-printed cardiac and thoracic cavity simulator for minimally invasive cardiac surgery
description: A life-like heart and thoracic cavity replica built from patient CT DICOM data converted to stereolithography data, designed in 3D CAD, printed as a mold, and cast in polyvinyl alcohol whose hardness and strength were tuned to measured tissue properties. The authors state that "PVA plays an important role in replicating the texture of the heart" and used the model to simulate minimally invasive mitral valve repair with real MICS tools and a robot.

constraints: The article states that accurate reproduction of each region would be expensive, so a cast-mold technique was used to produce a model comprising several parts

examples: The model was used with thoracotomy instruments, endoscope cameras, needle holders, and ports, and with the da Vinci Surgical System, to simulate MIMVR via left atriotomy

article_title: Approaches to studying predict academic performance in undergraduate occupational therapy students: a cross-cultural study.
citation: Bonsaksen T, Brown T, Lim HB, Fong K. (2017). Approaches to studying predict academic performance in undergraduate occupational therapy students: a cross-cultural study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-0914-3
title: Biggs' 3P model of learning in higher education (presage, process, product)
description: The article uses Biggs' 3P model as its organizing framework: a model of students' learning in higher education comprising presage, process, and product. "The presage factors are those that constitute the background and context for the learning experience", including sociodemographic characteristics and the situational context such as field of study, teaching and assessment forms, and time spent on tasks. The process is how students engage with study content, analysed via deep, surface and strategic approaches. The product (learning outcome) is seen as resulting from the interplay of student characteristics, learning environment and engagement.
requirements: The model presumes measures of student background, engagement approaches, and learning outcomes so their interplay can be examined
constraints: The article notes prior criticism that the deep versus surface learning dichotomy underpinning this line of work is overly simplistic
target_learning_goals: academic performance and understanding of study approaches
examples: The study operationalised presage as demographics and education factors, process as ASSIST subscale scores, and product as GPA

article_title: Effectiveness of a Low-Cost, Graduate Student-Led Intervention on Study Habits and Performance in Introductory Biology.
citation: Hoskins Tyler D., Gantz J. D., Chaffee Blake R., Arlinghaus Kel, Wiebler James, Hughes Michael, Fernandes Joyce J. (2017). title: BIO 104: an 8-week, pass/fail, graduate student–led metacognition-based study skills sprint course
description: BIO 104 is a low-cost supplemental course designed and taught by graduate TAs alongside introductory biology, requiring no faculty labor. It adapts the study cycle (Cook et al., 2013), teaching students to "study early and often, in short but intensive bouts," to make an outline after every lecture, and to construct concept maps from memory for self-assessment. TAs collected and graded one outline and one concept map weekly on 10-point content and organization scales with feedback.
requirements: Requires graduate TAs or advanced undergraduate facilitators willing to teach the course and grade weekly assignments
Requires students to voluntarily enroll after the first lecture exam
constraints: Enrollment is voluntary and self-selected, so results represent a self-selected group rather than a randomly selected cohort
Instructor-led, pre-exam study sessions were not part of the course
target_learners: First-year introductory biology students scoring ≤ 77% on the first lecture exam
target_learning_goals: Effective study habits and metacognitive self-assessment
Deep learning of introductory biology content
examples: TAs recruited students one week after exam 1 by visiting lecture sections, encouraged students earning ≤ 77% to enroll, and provided an electronic study log spreadsheet for tracking study hours

article_title: Concept Maps for Improved Science Reasoning and Writing: Complexity Isn't Everything.
citation: Dowd J.E., Duncan T., Reynolds J.A. (2015). Concept Maps for Improved Science Reasoning and Writing: Complexity Isn't Everything. CBE—Life Sciences Education 14(4). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.15-06-0138
title: BioTAP (Biology Thesis Assessment Protocol)
description: BioTAP is an assessment tool for "valid and reliable assessment of student writing," whose rubric addresses 13 dimensions of students' writing, nine of which concern writing and reasoning (e.g., argument for significance, interpretation of results, implications of findings). Each dimension is rated 1–5, where 5 indicates mastery. Two trained raters independently score each thesis, discuss discrepancies, and establish a discussion-based consensus score used in all analyses.
requirements: Rater training with sample writings illustrating inadequate, adequate, and masterful levels, plus calibration on sample theses before scoring
constraints: Prediscussion interrater Pearson correlation is 0.52 for total thesis scores, though dimension scores are within one point in ~80% of cases; consensus scores are 100% in agreement
target_learning_goals: scientific reasoning in writing
organization and presentation of thesis writing
examples: Used in this study to measure nine writing and reasoning dimensions for 49 theses, with total scores ranging from 32 to 44 out of 45
